sourceLine: your MentraOS work and the questions developers ask before they build for smart glasses

cards.title: Why the App Runtime Moved to the Phone
cards.angle: Meta opened Ray-Ban Display to third-party apps in May 2026 but runs them on the phone, not the glasses. Mentra reached the same architecture from the open-source side, and the reason is latency and ownership, not fashion.
cards.evidence: Your June 2026 roadmap post describes the old path (glasses to phone to cloud relay to developer app and back) and the control, privacy and OEM concerns it raised; Mentra 3.0 moved every miniapp onto the phone with offline STT and TTS. Confirm the round-trip figure with your engineers before it goes in a headline.

cards.title: Streaming Heat Is the Real Battery Ceiling
cards.angle: Meta says third-party apps cannot run on its glasses because of compute, thermal and battery limits. Your build log is the only public account of what that limit looks like on a bench.
cards.evidence: Your Making Mentra Live post describes the first chip overheating after extended high-quality streaming and the board redesign that separated WiFi from the processor; the product page rates 40+ minutes of livestreaming against 10+ hours mixed use. The ratio between those two numbers is the article.

sources.title: New Meta Developer Tool Enables Third-parties to Bring Apps to its Smart Glasses

cards.title: One Vendor Ships Two Thirds of Smart Glasses
cards.angle: IDC put Meta at 68.7 percent of Q2 2026 smart glasses shipments, and its developer program is a preview with no stated review process. An open OS is only an argument if it runs on hardware people can buy.
cards.evidence: MentraOS is Apache 2.0 with 2.3k GitHub stars and supports Mentra Live, Even Realities G1 and G2 and Vuzix Z100, and your first 1,000-unit batch sold out in under a month. No post on your site makes the platform-risk case to an enterprise buyer in those terms.
